claims.text: TiZrNbMoV-family refractory HEAs can be synthesized from near-equimolar elemental powder blends using LENS.
SEBM using elemental powder blends is a suitable fabrication strategy for Group IV-V refractory HEAs.
The AM material should receive a 24-hour vacuum homogenization treatment at 1000–1300 °C.
High-temperature homogenization at 1000–1300 °C dissolves segregation and reduces porosity.
A cryogenic treatment, low-temperature anneal, or rapid cooling step will refine the grain size after homogenization.
AM solidification of HEAs can involve cooling rates of 10^4–10^6 K/s.
The optimal state is a single-phase BCC solid solution with a grain size below 5 µm.
Controlling the AM cooling rate will suppress dendritic segregation and prevent brittle B2 or Laves phases.

Alloying Mo or W with Group IV or V transition metals changes the electronic structure, induces Jahn-Teller distortions, and changes the instability mode from tensile to shear failure, improving intrinsic ductility.
Reducing grain size improves plasticity or ductility in polycrystalline BCC metals.
Fine grains increase the alloy's strength through the Hall-Petch relationship.
Fine grains provide resistance to grain-boundary sliding and improve high-temperature creep behavior.
The SEBM vacuum environment minimizes oxygen, carbon, and nitrogen uptake.
Post-process heat treatment removes interstitials by diffusion or traps them in stable carbides and nitrides, thereby preventing embrittlement.
Trace aluminum or oxygen commonly induces brittle B2 or Laves phases in these alloys.
Conventional refractory HEAs generally combine low room-temperature ductility with high strength.
The proposed AM RHEA will achieve more than 10% room-temperature tensile ductility.
The proposed AM RHEA will achieve a room-temperature yield strength above 800 MPa.
At 1000 °C, the alloy will retain more than 80% of its room-temperature yield strength.
At 1000 °C, the alloy will exhibit negligible creep relative to conventional Ni-based superalloys.

contradictions.description: Fine grain size is said both to provide resistance to grain-boundary sliding and to facilitate grain-boundary sliding. These imply opposite effects unless different temperature or deformation regimes are specified.
The baseline identifies grain-boundary sliding as a limitation on high-temperature strength, whereas the mechanism says facilitating grain-boundary sliding maintains structural integrity.
